description.value: The study examined task-related vmPFC-amygdala functional connectivity during passive viewing of negative and neutral images in adolescents, including associations with childhood abuse and later psychopathology.

spans.text: The present study investigates whether exposure to child abuse influences functional connectivity between the vmPFC and amygdala during a passive emotional processing task among adolescents.

value: We hypothesized that adolescents who had been exposed to abuse would show a more negative pattern of task-related functional connectivity between vmPFC and amygdala, that this pattern would be associated with higher levels of internalizing and externalizing psychopathology, and that this negative pattern of task-related functional connectivity would mediate the relationship between child abuse and later psychopathology.

value: Task-related functional connectivity to the left amygdala was more strongly negative during trials involving negative as compared to neutral stimuli in a right vmPFC cluster encompassing mOFC and sgACC.

Exposure to abuse was associated with more negative task-related functional connectivity of the left amygdala with both vmPFC clusters, and more negative connectivity was associated with higher concurrent externalizing psychopathology and with externalizing psychopathology two years later.

The authors interpreted this pattern as potentially reflecting disengagement of regulatory responses from vmPFC when amygdala reactivity is high, possibly due to stronger threat appraisals following childhood abuse.
